content.summary_of_the_paper:
This manuscript tackles a generalized category discovery setting and mostly focuses on estimating the number of unknown classes.
The authors propose an EM-like framework that alternates between prototype estimation with a variant of GMM (E-step) and representation learning based on prototypical contrastive learning (M-step).
Empirical results on generic and fine-grained image classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- This manuscript focuses on a very interesting perspective in automatically deciding the number of unknown classes. The attempt and resulting method looks novel to me.

- Table 4 and Figure 4 look very promising and fundamentally interesting. I'm wondering if the authors have any insights/explanation on why the two curves all go down a bit in late training stage. Besides, I feel it would be more comprehensive if the authors could additionally provide figures that have initially more classes than the exact number.

- How does the proposed method addresses unknown classes if the distribution is imbalanced?

- How does the proposed method addresses noisy examples that potentially doesn't belong to any cluster?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Does the authors use the same backbone (ViT) across all baselines?

- How to interpret Table 10? Why the standard deviation are all integers?

- It's unclear to me how the merge process works with $H_m$. How does the proposed method determine which two clusters to merge with $H_m$, as it seems to me that $H_m$ only conditions on cluster i.

- What's the runtime analysis of the proposed method?

- What's the intuition of using eq (5) as Hastings ratio? What's the distribution estimated under this Hastings ratio?
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting results on automatically learning the number of unknown clusters. The presentation of this work is yet not very clear though.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper devotes to handling the problem of generalized category discovery (GCD), which leverages the labeled images to classify the unlabeled images. In contrast to previous works, this paper considers a realistic scenario that the number of categories of unlabeled images is unknown. Specifically, this paper proposes an EM-like framework called GPC, where the E-step estimates the classes of unlabeled data and a set of prototypes by a semi-supervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM), and the M-step utilizes the determined categories and prototypes to learn representation with contrastive learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper proposes a semi-supervised Gaussian mixture model with the stochastic splitting and merging mechanism to dynamically determine the class number and cluster data. I think this contribution is interesting.
2. This paper is very well written.

Weakness:
1. This paper claims that class number estimation and representation learning can reinforce each other in the learning process, and considers it as a contribution. However, the marriage between representation learning and clustering methods is too common in many fields, such as learning with noisy learning [1] and open-set recognition [2]. Therefore, it is insufficient to be a point of novelty or contribution. 
2. The paper combines prototypical contrastive learning (PCL) with contrastive learning (CL) to improve the representation. What if there is only CL generating representations without PCL, or there is only PCL? The related experiments are needed.
3. The combination of PCL and CL is not novel enough, where [3] has combined CL and PCL to learn robust representation. 
4. The setting of the paper is quite similar to that of open-set semi-supervised learning (SSL), and the authors’ evaluation metric is also very similar to that of open-set SSL (i.e., the evaluation metric in this paper is the accuracy on classifying both known and unknown data, and open-set SSL aims to classify known data correctly while rejecting unknown data). In general, open-set SSL treats all unknown categories as one class, i.e., the outlier. So why not discuss open-set SSL and maybe compare the accuracy of your method on known data with that of other open-set SSL methods [4], [5], [6], [7]? 

[1] Wang Y, Liu W, Ma X, et al. Iterative learning with open-set noisy labels[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2018: 8688-8696.

[2] Huang J, Fang C, Chen W, et al. Trash to Treasure: Harvesting OOD Data with Cross-Modal Matching for Open-Set Semi-Supervised Learning[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021: 8310-8319.

[3] Li J, Xiong C, Hoi S C H. Learning from noisy data with robust representation learning[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021: 9485-9494.

[4] Guo L Z, Zhang Z Y, Jiang Y, et al. Safe deep semi-supervised learning for unseen-class unlabeled data[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020: 3897-3906.

[5] Yu Q, Ikami D, Irie G, et al. Multi-task curriculum framework for open-set semi-supervised learning[C]//European Conference on Computer Vision. Springer, Cham, 2020: 438-454.

[6] Saito K, Kim D, Saenko K. OpenMatch: Open-set Consistency Regularization for Semi-supervised Learning with Outliers[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2105.14148, 2021.

[7] Chen Y, Zhu X, Li W, et al. Semi-supervised learning under class distribution mismatch[C]//Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. 2020, 34(04): 3569-3576.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The presentation of this paper is generally clear.

Quality:
This paper clearly describes how to implement the overall framework and conducts intensive experimental verification. Therefore, this paper has good technical quality. However, this paper does not explain why the proposed contrastive learning is beneficial for GMM to determine unlabeled data. The theoretical quality of this paper is unconvincing.

Novelty:
This paper aims to solve the GCD problem, where the number the categories of unlabeled data is unknown. However, the motivation of this paper is lacking. For example, the paper argues that class number estimation and representation learning can reinforce each other in the learning process. However, how the combined contrastive learning improves the GMM has not been illustrated in either theory or experiments.

Reproducibility:
The pseudo-algorithm and implementation details of the proposed method are clearly described. Therefore, I think this paper is easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: A combination or adaptation of some existing works to solve a more realistic GCD problem; some components lack explanation in theory and experiments.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of  generalized category discovery (GCD). To solve this problem, an EM-like framework is proposed to alternates between representation learning and class number estimation. Specifically, a semi-supervised Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) is presented to discovery prototypes for contrastive learning. Experiments on several datasets show the benefit of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

+ This paper considers a newly proposed problem, which is a practical task.

+ This paper is well-written and easy to follow.

+ An effective approach is proposed for the new task, which significantly improves the performance.

+ Extensive experiments are provided to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Weaknesses

- Despite the good performance, the novelty of the proposed method is limited. Both EM-like learning and prototypical learning are widely studied in the semi-supervised learning. I did not find too much new techniques from the proposed method.

- The proposed GMM is largely similar to [A]. What is the difference between the proposed GMM and [A]? It seems that the this paper directly applies [A] to GCD and name it as GMM.

[A] Meitar Ronen, Shahaf E. Finder, and Oren Freifeld. Deepdpm: Deep clustering with an unknown
number of clusters. In CVPR, 2022. 

- Although the overall writing is good, the description of Sec.3.2 is hard to understand.

- The improvement over Vaze et al. (2022a)  commonly is limited, while the proposed method is much more complex and requires more training stages.

- I found that the  Zhong et al. (2021a) also utilizes contrastive learning for NCD. Thus, the authors should provide a comparison with this method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality: The overall writing is good except for the sec 3.2.

Novelty: Despite the good performance, the EM-like framework and prototypical learning in the proposed method are not novel.

Reproducibility: The training process seems complex. I think one can hardly reproduce the results without source code.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper considers a new, interesting task and proposes an effective approach to solve it. However, the novelty of the proposed method is somewhat limited: the EM-like training framework is widely used and the proposed GMMs is very similar to [A]. In addition, with more computation cost or training process, the proposed method does not lead too much improvements over Vaze et al. (2022a). I thus tend to give borderline reject.

content.title: General Response (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their insightful and constructive comments. We are encouraged to see that our work is thought to be considered a practical and realistic task (Reviewer AdbJ and rVTs), our paper is well-written and clear (Reviewer AdbJ and rVTs), our method significantly improves the performance and is an interesting and novel contribution (Reviewer AdbJ, rVTS, and ubLN). We considered the suggestions and will include them in the revision of our paper.

We address the key concerns of the reviewers below:

>Q1: The novelty of our work (Reviewer AbdJ)
>
>A1: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the related work, we have already cited and discussed this paper in our paper, and we would like to highlight the key difference with [A] here:
>Our method considers a different question than [A], namely Generalized Category Discovery where a set of labelled data is given which can be considered as the criteria for clustering, compared to unsupervised clustering evaluated in [A] where the cluster criteria can be formed arbitrary, GCD is a more realistic setting.
>GMM is a widely adopted technique among many fields, in our work, we modify the GMM to a partially supervised setting tailored for the problem of GCD, and adopted the split and merging technique from [A].

>Q2: Performance improvements over Vaze etal are limited (Reviewer AbdJ)
>
>A2: We would like to clarify that our method can indeed improve the performance of Vaze etal, in Tab. 2 and 3, we show the performance of the original Vaze etal baseline as well as the performance of using the PCA layer on top of Vaze etal, we have observed a performance improvement of the PCA layer for Vaze etal.
>For our combined framework, together with the PCA and the prototypical contrastive learning, our method can outperform Vaze etal by a noticeable margin, comparing row 5 with row 7 and row 8 with row 11 in table 2 and 3.

>Q3: Comparison with Noisy learning and open-set recognition. (Reviewer rVTs)
>
>A3: Thanks for pointing out these related fields, we would like to clarify that noisy learning, open-set recognition, and generalized category discovery are all open-world learning scenarios, the challenges they face are different from each other, in the generalized category discovery setting, the main challenge is how to robustly estimate the number of categories as well as assign labels to each unlabelled data points while estimating the number of categories is not a challenge for noisy learning or open-set recognition settings.


>Q4: Discussion with open-set SSL works. (Reviewer rVTs)
>
>A4: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the related works on open-set SSL, these are indeed related to the problem of generalized category discovery, we will cite and discuss these papers, however, we would like to note that our main focus is to discover the novel categories in the unlabelled set at the meantime maintain the performance on old categories, thus we do not expect our method to outperform the open-set SSL methods on the old categories, but we do expect a reasonably good performance on the old categories with our classifier as we already show that our method can outperform other GCD methods on the old categories under the GCD setting. We will consider further boosting the performance of the old categories by introducing the techniques from open-set SSL methods.

>Q5: The influence of using more initial classes than GT, and the influence of imbalance class distribution. (Reviewer ubLN)
>
>A5: Thanks for the suggestions, we have performed the experiments of using more initial classes than GT, and found that during the training process the estimated number of classes is always higher than GT and finally converges to a higher number than GT. Overall our method would overestimate the number of classes in the dataset.
For the influence of imbalance class distribution, we will perform further experiments on the Herbarium19 dataset which is a long-tailed dataset and has been used by Vaze etal to validate the effectiveness of generalized category discovery methods. The results will be included in future revision.

content.title: General Response (2/2)
content.comment:
>Q6: How do the merging process work and the intuition of Eq 5. (Reviewer ubLN)
>
> A6: Thanks for the question, we are sorry this is not clear in the first place, we would like to clarify that for the merging process, the H_m is implemented as H_m = \frac{\Gamma(N_i + N_j) h(\mathcal{Z}_{i}\cup \mathcal{Z}_j; \theta)}{\Gamma(N_{i})h(\mathcal{Z}_{i};\theta) \Gamma(N_{j})h(\mathcal{Z}_{j};\theta)}, where the ratio is conditioned on two clusters i and j which are considered for merging.
For the intuition behind Eq 5, we would like to clarify that Eq 5. is the probability of accepting the split proposal for one cluster, the $\Gamma$ terms in Eq 5. are measuring the number of data points within each sub-cluster, and the $h(Z;\theta)$ terms are measuring the marginal likelihood of the two sub-clusters, ie how independent of the two sub-clusters. Intuitively, when the two sub-clusters have mostly equal number of data and their marginal likelihood function values are high, the two sub-clusters are more likely to be split into two clusters. 

After careful consideration, we have decided to withdraw our work, and we thank the reviewers for their constructive comments and will include these discussions in the future revision of our work.
